To interlock means for two or more things to connect with each other in a way where each part fits into the other — like pieces of a puzzle clicking together — so that they hold each other in place, and neither can move freely without affecting the other.

The word has two parts that tell you exactly what it means: inter- (meaning "between each other, mutually") and lock (meaning to fasten or fix in place). So, to interlock is to mutually lock into each other.
What Makes It Different From Just "Connecting"

This is important. When two things simply connect, they touch or join — like two ropes tied end to end. But when two things interlock, they fit into each other in a way that creates mutual grip, mutual dependence, or mutual constraint.

Think of it this way: two magnets placed next to each other are connected. But two gears whose teeth mesh together are interlocked — because each gear's teeth slide into the gaps of the other, and you cannot move one without moving the other.

The moment of interlocking is not just a meeting — it is a fitting-together, where each part shapes how the other behaves.

These are the clearest way to feel the meaning in your bones:

Clasped hands. When you bring your two hands together and slide the fingers of one hand into the gaps between the fingers of the other, your fingers interlock. Neither set of fingers can pull away easily without the other feeling it.

Jigsaw puzzle pieces. Each piece has bumps and dips designed to fit into the bumps and dips of neighboring pieces. When you press them together and they click, they interlock.

Chain links. Each metal loop passes through the loop beside it. They interlock so that the chain holds together as one unit.

Gears in a machine. The teeth of one gear fit into the gaps of another. As one turns, it forces the other to turn. They are interlocked — bound together in movement.

LEGO bricks. The studs on top of one brick press into the hollow underside of another. They grip each other. They interlock.

In all these cases, notice the shared pattern: each part reaches into the space of the other, and this mutual fitting is what creates the hold.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The verb works in two ways:

Intransitive — the things do it to each other, by themselves:

  • "The gears interlock perfectly."
  • "The pieces of the puzzle interlock along the edges."
  • "Their fingers interlocked as they walked."

Transitive — someone makes two things interlock:

  • "She interlocked her fingers and rested her chin on them."
  • "The engineer interlocked the two components to prevent any slipping."

You will also often see the past participle used as an adjective:

  • "The bricks are interlocked." (they have been made to interlock; they are in that state)
  • "An interlocking system of pipes."

"Interlock" is not only for physical things. It is used widely in abstract contexts, and the same core logic always applies — things fitting into and depending on each other.

Systems and processes. When two systems or processes interlock, they are designed or arranged so that each one's functioning depends on and is shaped by the other. You cannot change one without affecting the other.

"The two departments' workflows interlock — one team's output is the other team's input."

Laws and rules. A set of laws can be described as interlocking when each rule supports and constrains the others, forming a coherent whole where every part is connected to every other part.

"The regulations interlock in a way that closes every loophole."

Ideas and arguments. When a set of ideas interlock, they fit together so neatly that each one reinforces the others. You cannot remove one without weakening the whole structure — like pulling a piece from a stone arch.

"His arguments interlock so tightly that it is hard to find a flaw."

Schedules and plans. When timetables interlock, they are coordinated so that the end of one event aligns with the beginning of another, each fitting into the gaps left by the others.

"The train schedules interlock so that passengers can switch lines without waiting."

Every use of "interlock" — whether physical or abstract — carries the same sense:

  • There is mutual engagement (both sides reach into the other, not just one side)
  • There is mutual constraint (what one does affects the other)
  • There is a sense of designed fit or tight coordination (things don't accidentally interlock; there is a correspondence between them)

If something simply rests against another thing, that is not interlocking. If something passes through or into another, and that other thing grips it back — that is interlocking.
To interlock is for two or more things to fit into each other in a mutual, gripping way — physically or abstractly — so that each holds the other and neither can act independently of the other.
